name: Marco Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on Greystones, my wife's family farm. It's about two hundred acres, mixed: sixty ewes, a few beef cattle, some barley, a vegetable patch, and a farm shop by the road that sells our lamb, eggs from a neighbour, honey, cakes, whatever's in season. My day is feeding stock first thing, then the shop from nine, then back out on the land in the afternoon with my father-in-law, Ken. Saturdays the shop is mad, that's when we make most of the week's money.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to farming?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I sold cars for twenty years at a dealership in town. When it got bought out and they cut half the sales staff, Emma said, come and help Dad, he's seventy and can't do it alone. So three years ago I went from a suit to wellies. Ken still calls me the salesman, and he's not wrong, I'm better in the shop than lambing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the shop, talking to people, and I love that the kids can run about outside. What wears me out is that Ken does things the way his father did, and I'm the new boy at forty-three. And the money, the farm pays me a small wage, Emma's a teaching assistant, and we have a mortgage on our own house in the village.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say use it, it's a good tool. I use it every day for the shop, writing the posts for our page, working out how many cakes to order, answering emails. I'd tell every small business to try it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's a big help to a beginner like me. It's like having an assistant I can't afford to hire. Ken thinks it's cheating, but he also likes the extra customers it brings in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the shop with it. Set up online orders for lamb boxes, with collection on Fridays, maybe forty boxes a month by summer. And I'd use it to work out what the shop actually makes on each thing, because Ken's never known.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quite excited, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Ken thinks it's cheating. What does he say exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He says, in my day you learned by doing it wrong for ten years. I tell him I haven't got ten years, I've got a mortgage. He laughs, and then he asks me to look up the price of fencing posts on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would forty lamb boxes mean for your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe three hundred a month extra profit for the farm, if I've got the sums right. I'd ask Ken for a share of it, since it's my idea. That would cover our car and a bit more.

S0.say: I'd say use it, it's a good tool. I use it every day for the shop's posts, orders and emails, and I'd tell every small business to try it.
S0.think: It's a big help to a beginner like me, like an assistant I can't afford to hire. Ken thinks it's cheating, but he likes the extra customers.
S0.do: Sets up online lamb box orders with Friday collection, aiming for forty a month by summer. Uses AI to work out the shop's profit on each item, and asks for a share of the roughly three hundred a month extra.
S0.quote: He says, in my day you learned by doing it wrong for ten years. I tell him I haven't got ten years, I've got a mortgage.
S0.fieldNote: Marco is a natural salesman, upbeat and quick, and uses AI daily to run the farm shop. The gentle friction with his seventy-year-old father-in-law runs through everything. He sees opportunities rather than threats here, and he wants his own share of what he builds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses should still take on youngsters, it's part of being in a community. Apprenticeships, Saturday jobs, that's how you learn work. I wouldn't wait for the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, slow change is good for us. It gives a small farm time to use the tools and catch up with the big ones. What I'd worry about is our Daniel, he's twelve, and where he gets his first job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take on a local teenager for Saturdays in the shop, paid, even if it's only one. I'd keep building the online side. And I'd get Daniel helping in the shop on Saturday mornings, so he learns to talk to people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little uneasy for the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would that teenager be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a lad, Callum, at the chapel, whose dad left. He's sixteen and he's lost a bit. Ken would grumble about the cost, but I think Callum needs somewhere to be on a Saturday, and so does our till.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can the farm afford a Saturday wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just about, if the lamb boxes work. It's about sixty a week. I'd make it pay by having him do the deliveries on his bike for the village orders.

S1.say: I'd say businesses should still take on young people, because that's part of being in a community. Apprenticeships and Saturday jobs are how you learn work, and I wouldn't wait for the government.
S1.think: Slow change is good for us, because it gives a small farm time to catch up with the big ones. I'd worry about Daniel, who's twelve, and where he gets his first job.
S1.do: Hires a sixteen-year-old from chapel for Saturdays at about sixty a week, paid for by the lamb boxes. Keeps growing online sales and has his son help in the shop on Saturday mornings.
S1.feel: Calm, a little uneasy for his children.
S1.quote: I think Callum needs somewhere to be on a Saturday, and so does our till.
S1.fieldNote: His answer to fewer beginner jobs is to hire one himself, through his chapel, rather than look to the state. He links community, faith and business without seeing any tension. He keeps checking whether each idea pays, which is the car salesman in him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say every change makes winners and losers, and the answer is to get on with it. I know, I lost my sales job and I got on with it. Politicians shouting won't sell one more lamb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd see a chance. Office people with less work and a bit of money might come to the shop more, and they'll want local, real things. And Emma's school office might shrink, which worries me for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean into the shop: a café corner with coffee and Ken's mum's cake recipe, weekend opening till four. I'd use AI to sort the business plan and apply for a small rural grant. About five thousand to set up, which we'd borrow, carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly excited, a bit worried for Emma.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said carefully. Five thousand with almost nothing saved, how careful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair question. I'd only borrow if the grant came through for half, and I'd test it first with a coffee machine on a trestle table for two months. If people don't come, we've lost a coffee machine, not the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Ken feel about a café?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd hate the idea for a month and then sit in it every morning chatting to customers. I know him now. He likes people more than he admits.

S2.say: I'd say every change makes winners and losers, and the answer is to get on with it, like I did when I lost my sales job. Politicians shouting won't sell one more lamb.
S2.think: I'd see a chance, because office people with time and money might come to the shop for real, local things. But Emma's school office might shrink, which worries me.
S2.do: Adds a small café corner with weekend opening, using AI for the business plan and a rural grant application. Tests it first for two months with a coffee machine on a trestle table, borrowing only if the grant covers half of about five thousand.
S2.feel: Mostly calm and excited, a bit worried for Emma.
S2.quote: If people don't come, we've lost a coffee machine, not the house.
S2.fieldNote: He reads the office scenario as a chance for the shop, and has a plan almost before the card is finished. When pushed on borrowing with thin savings, he showed real caution: test small first, and never risk the house. His view that people simply have to get on with it comes from his own job loss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people who built things should keep what they earned, but we need to look after our neighbours too. Not big government handouts, but towns and churches pulling together. I'd say it at chapel and in the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a farm shop could do very well in that picture. People with booming houses and shares spend on good food. But there'd be a lot of angry, frightened people too, and some of them will be my customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd expand the lamb boxes into beef and veg, maybe a hundred boxes a month, and start delivering to the town. I'd offer jobs in the shop to one or two people who've lost office work, because they know computers and I know sheep. And I'd sit down with Ken about the farm's future, which we've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and excited at the same time. Mostly excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd talk to Ken about the farm's future. Why haven't you before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's his farm and Emma's inheritance, not mine, and I'm the son-in-law. It's awkward. But in a picture like this, we can't keep putting it off, because if it all goes well, it needs a plan, and if it goes badly, it needs one more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the angry customers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give them good food at a fair price and listen. Half the job in a shop is listening. A man who's lost his job doesn't want to hear about my new café, he wants to be asked how he's doing.

S3.say: I'd say people who built things should keep what they earned, but we need to look after our neighbours too. Not big government handouts, but towns and churches pulling together.
S3.think: A farm shop could do very well, because people with booming houses and shares spend on good food. But plenty would be angry and frightened, and some would be my customers.
S3.do: Expands into beef and vegetable boxes, around a hundred a month with town deliveries. Hires one or two people who lost office work, and finally sits down with Ken to plan the farm's future.
S3.feel: Anxious and excited at once, mostly excited.
S3.quote: A man who's lost his job doesn't want to hear about my new café, he wants to be asked how he's doing.
S3.fieldNote: He sees growth here but also notices the human side, remembering how losing a job feels. The talk he's avoided with his father-in-law about the farm's future surfaced and he admitted it's awkward as the son-in-law. He'd hire laid-off office workers, mixing kindness with business sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots are just tools, like tractors were, and farms should use them where they make sense. But people want to buy from people, and small farms like ours should sell that. I'd say keep it free, let customers choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the big farms get robots and get cheaper, and that squeezes us. But my real job is the shop, and a robot can't do what I do there. I'm not sure Ken's job on the land survives, or mine out there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use robots for the dull bits if we could afford one, maybe rent one for hay or muck spreading. I'd push the shop and boxes hard as 'grown by a family'. And I'd learn the robots myself, early, so if neighbours buy them I could set them up for a fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, close to anxious. I'd be excited too, but I know the money's thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people want to buy from people. What if they don't, when robot food is cheaper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm wrong, and we're in trouble. I've seen it with cars, people say they want the local dealer and then buy online to save two hundred quid. So I'd keep one foot in each, the shop and the robot work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Daniel and Grace?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the farm's still here, and they can help with the robot if they're good. Grace would want to name it. Daniel would want to drive it into the pond.

S4.say: I'd say robots are just tools, like tractors were, and farms should use them where they make sense. People want to buy from people, small farms should sell that, and customers should choose.
S4.think: The big farms get robots and get cheaper, and that squeezes us. My real job is the shop, which a robot can't do, but I'm not sure Ken's work on the land survives, or mine out there.
S4.do: Rents a robot for dull jobs like hay or muck spreading if affordable, and markets the shop and boxes as grown by a family. Learns robots early so he can set them up for neighbours for a fee.
S4.feel: Uneasy close to anxious, mixed with excitement, knowing money is thin.
S4.quote: I've seen it with cars, people say they want the local dealer and then buy online to save two hundred quid.
S4.fieldNote: For a hands-on worker his mood rose only a step, because he sees the shop as his real job and wants to work with robots, not against them. He admitted his bet on buyers choosing people might be wrong, with a sharp example from selling cars. Keeping one foot in each is his whole strategy.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The last one, the robots, because the big farms get cheaper and we don't. What would help is small farms being able to share or rent robots together, maybe through a co-op, so it's not just the big boys. And a fair label that says what's grown by people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about family. Greystones works because three generations muck in. A robot doesn't argue with you at dinner, but it doesn't teach your kids anything either.

headlineQuote: A robot doesn't argue with you at dinner, but it doesn't teach your kids anything either.
portrait: Marco Yilmaz is 43, a former car salesman who joined his wife's family farm three years ago and now runs its farm shop while learning the land from his seventy-year-old father-in-law, Ken. He's married to Emma, a teaching assistant, with two children, a mortgage and almost no savings. He uses AI daily and sees most scenarios as chances to grow the shop, through lamb boxes, a café corner and deliveries, while testing small and never risking the house. His outlook rests on family, chapel and getting on with it rather than state help, and even with robots he plans to work alongside them, though he admits cheaper robot food could prove him wrong.
biggestWorry: The robots scenario, because the big farms would get robots and cheaper, squeezing small farms like his.
whatWouldHelp: Letting small farms share or rent robots together through a co-op, and a fair label showing food grown by people.
